spacex-overview.text: Falcon 9 is a reusable, two-stage rocket made by SpaceX that carries people and payloads into Earth orbit.
spacex-overview.quote: Falcon 9 is a reusable, two-stage rocket designed and manufactured by SpaceX for the reliable and safe transport of people and payloads into Earth orbit and beyond.

spacex-reuse.text: Reusability lets SpaceX fly the most expensive parts of the rocket again.
spacex-reuse.quote: Reusability allows SpaceX to refly the most expensive parts of the rocket, which in turn drives down the cost of space access.

spacex-dimensions.text: Falcon 9 is 70 m tall and 3.7 m across, and weighs 549,054 kg at liftoff.
spacex-dimensions.quote: HEIGHT 70 m / 229.6 ft DIAMETER 3.7 m / 12 ft MASS 549,054 kg / 1,207,920 lbs

spacex-first-stage.text: The first stage has nine Merlin engines and aluminium-lithium tanks of liquid oxygen and rocket-grade kerosene (RP-1).
spacex-first-stage.quote: Falcon 9's first stage incorporates nine Merlin engines and aluminum-lithium alloy tanks containing liquid oxygen and rocket-grade kerosene (RP-1) propellant.

guide-nine-engines.text: Each of the nine first-stage engines gives up to 845 kN at sea level.
guide-nine-engines.quote: Nine SpaceX M1D engines power the Falcon 9 first stage with up to 845 kN (190,000 lbf) thrust per engine at sea level

guide-engine-layout.text: The nine engines sit in a circle of eight round a centre engine.
guide-engine-layout.quote: The first stage M1D engines are configured in a circular pattern, with eight engines surrounding a center engine.

guide-throttle.text: The first-stage engines throttle from 190,000 lbf down to 108,300 lbf each.
guide-throttle.quote: Throttle capability Yes (190,000 lbf to 108,300 lbf sea level)

guide-common-dome.text: A common dome separates the LOX and RP-1 tanks; a transfer tube carries LOX through the RP-1 tank to the engines.
guide-common-dome.quote: A common dome separates the LOX and RP-1 tanks, and a double-wall transfer tube carries LOX through the center of the RP-1 tank to the engine section.

guide-fins-legs.text: Four grid fins near the top of the first stage and four deployable legs at its base are flown for recovery.
guide-fins-legs.quote: Four grid fins near the top of the first stage along with four deployable legs at the base are nominally flown to support recovery operations.

guide-held-down.text: After the engines start, the rocket is held down until its systems check out, then released.
guide-held-down.quote: After engine start, Falcon vehicles are held down until all vehicle systems are verified as functioning normally before release for liftoff.

guide-nitrogen-thrusters.text: Cold nitrogen gas thrusters point and roll the stages; on the first stage they are used for recovery.
guide-nitrogen-thrusters.quote: Coast attitude control Nitrogen gas thrusters (recovery only) Nitrogen gas thrusters

guide-separation.text: The stages are latched at three points; after the first-stage engines shut down, helium releases the latches and four pneumatic pushers push the stages apart.
guide-separation.quote: After the first stage engines shut down, a high -pressure helium circuit is used to release the latches via redundant actuators. The helium system also preloads four pneumatic pushers, which provide a positive force for stage separation after latch release.

guide-fairing-halves.text: The fairing is two halves latched along a seam; helium releases them and four pneumatic pushers push them away.
guide-fairing-halves.quote: To deploy the fairing, a high -pressure helium circuit releases the latches, and four pneumatic pushers facilitate positive-force deployment of the two halves.

guide-timeline.text: A sample flight: liftoff at T+0, max Q at T+74 s, main engine cutoff at T+147 s, stage separation at T+151 s, second engine start at T+158 s, fairing separation at T+222 s.
guide-timeline.quote: T + 74 s Maximum dynamic pressure (max Q) T + 147 s Main engine cutoff (MECO) T + 151 s Stage separation T + 158 s Second engine start-1 (SES-1) T + 222 s Fairing separation

guide-throttled-in-flight.text: The engines may be throttled in flight to keep loads within limits.
guide-throttled-in-flight.quote: Both the first and second stage engines may be throttled to help maintain launch vehicle and payload steady state acceleration limits.

maxq-throttle-down.text: The engines ease back round max Q, the moment of greatest air pressure on the rocket.
maxq-throttle-down.note: Max Q is in the guide's timeline and the guide says the engines may be throttled to keep loads within limits; throttling down round max Q follows from that and from the model's own pressure peak. The guide does not state it for max Q.

spacex-interstage.text: The interstage is a composite structure that joins the stages and holds the pneumatic pushers that separate them.
spacex-interstage.quote: The interstage is a composite structure that connects the first and second stages, and houses the pneumatic pushers that allow the first and second stage to separate during flight.

spacex-grid-fins.text: Four grid fins at the base of the interstage steer the booster on the way back down by moving its centre of pressure.
spacex-grid-fins.quote: Falcon 9 is equipped with four hypersonic grid fins positioned at the base of the interstage. They orient the rocket during reentry by moving the center of pressure.

spacex-second-stage.text: The second stage has one Merlin Vacuum engine that lights a few seconds after separation and carries the payload to orbit.
spacex-second-stage.quote: The second stage, powered by a single Merlin Vacuum Engine, delivers Falcon 9's payload to the desired orbit. The second stage engine ignites a few seconds after stage separation

guide-mvac-nozzle.text: The Merlin Vacuum engine has a fixed nozzle with a 165:1 expansion ratio.
guide-mvac-nozzle.quote: A single Merlin Vacuum (MVac) engine powers the second stage, using a fixed 165:1 expansion nozzle.

spacex-fairing.text: The carbon-composite fairing, 13.1 m tall and 5.2 m across, protects the satellites and is dropped about three minutes into flight.
spacex-fairing.quote: Made of a carbon composite material, the fairing protects satellites on their way to orbit. The fairing is jettisoned approximately 3 minutes into flight

spacex-fairing-size.quote: HEIGHT 13.1 m / 43 ft DIAMETER 5.2 m / 17.1 ft

wiki-recovery-burns.text: After separation the booster flips round; an optional boostback burn reverses its course, an entry burn slows it before the thick air, and a landing burn brings it down to touchdown.
wiki-recovery-burns.quote: After stage separation, the booster flips around (an optional boostback burn reverses its course), a reentry burn sheds gravity-induced speed to prevent stage overheating as the spacecraft reenters the thicker part of the atmosphere, and a landing burn accomplishes the final low-altitude deceleration and touchdown.

asds-barge.text: A droneship is a modified ocean-going barge with its own propulsion to hold position and a large landing platform.
asds-barge.quote: An autonomous spaceport drone ship (ASDS) is a modified ocean-going barge developed by SpaceX and equipped with propulsion systems to maintain precise position and a large landing platform.

wiki-crs8-landing.text: A Falcon 9 booster first landed on a droneship on the CRS-8 flight in April 2016.
wiki-crs8-landing.quote: Flight 23, CRS-8 — first successful landing on an autonomous spaceport drone ship.

model-values.text: Heights, speeds, throttle and the recovery burn times come from a small flat-Earth model with chosen masses, drag and burn plan.
model-values.note: Liftoff mass, thrust per engine, throttle floor and the ascent event times are sourced; stage masses, specific impulse, drag areas, pitch program, boostback length, entry burn and the landing guidance are chosen so the flight behaves sensibly. Numbers after separation are not a real mission's.

drawing-proportions.text: Lengths of the tanks, interstage and engines are estimated from the sourced height, diameters and fairing size.
drawing-proportions.note: The total height, the 3.66 m and 5.2 m diameters and the 13.1 m fairing are sourced; the LOX tank is drawn above the RP-1 tank as the transfer tube implies; the split of lengths between them is estimated.

film-compression.text: The film compresses the flight in time and draws distances to the pad and droneship on a squeezed scale.
film-compression.note: A drawing choice: the eight-minute flight plays in about 26 s at a varying rate, and the scenery moves on a scale that saturates so the pad and ship stay findable.

thruster-place.text: The nitrogen thruster pods are drawn near the top of the interstage.
thruster-place.note: The guide names nitrogen thrusters on both stages but does not draw them; their place on the first stage near the grid fins is from photographs and is not sourced here.

guide-slc40.text: SpaceX launches Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral, with a launch pad and lightning towers.
guide-slc40.quote: SpaceX facilities at SLC-40 (Figure 8-1) include a launch vehicle integration hangar, propellant and pressurant storage and supply areas, a launch pad, and lightning towers.

guide-lightning-wires.text: The SLC-40 and LC-39A pads have overhead wire lightning protection.
guide-lightning-wires.quote: The SLC-40 and LC-39A launch pads are equipped with overhead wire lightning protection systems.

guide-strongback.text: The transporter-erector strongback is pulled back just before launch.
guide-strongback.quote: The transporter-erector strongback is retracted just prior to launch.

guide-clamps.text: Engines light while hydraulic clamps hold the rocket at its base; the clamps release at T-0.
guide-clamps.quote: Engine ignition occurs shortly before liftoff, while the vehicle is held down at the base via hydraulic clamps. The flight computer evaluates engine ignition and full-power performance during the prelaunch hold-down, and if nominal criteria are satisfied, the hydraulic release system is activated at T-0.

wiki-shock-diamonds.text: Shock diamonds are standing wave patterns in a supersonic exhaust plume, seen when the engine runs in an atmosphere.
wiki-shock-diamonds.quote: Shock diamonds (also known as Mach diamonds or thrust diamonds, and less commonly Mach disks) are a formation of standing wave patterns that appear in the supersonic exhaust plume of an aerospace propulsion system, such as a supersonic jet engine, rocket, ramjet, or scramjet, when it is operated in an atmosphere.

pad-drawing.text: The launch mount, flame trench and the places of the towers are drawn after photographs of the pad, simplified, with the lightning towers closer to the rocket than they stand.
pad-drawing.note: The guide names the pad, lightning towers with overhead wires, the transporter-erector and the hold-down clamps; photographs show the layout but not the trench inside, so the trench is a plain duct opening on the side away from the erector, and the tower pairs are drawn about 30 m either side instead of the larger real spacing.

plume-drawing.text: Exhaust flames, shock diamonds and the cloud at liftoff are drawn effects driven by the model throttle and altitude, not measured shapes.
plume-drawing.note: Shock diamonds are sourced for a plume in an atmosphere; the core, the widening with altitude and the cloud are drawn after common launch footage, not from a measurement.

wiki-slc40-crew-tower.text: Since 2023 SLC-40 has its own access tower, first used for a crew launch in September 2024.
wiki-slc40-crew-tower.quote: To add additional operational flexibility and reduce reliance on LC-39A, in early 2023, SpaceX began constructing an access tower at SLC-40.

wiki-slc40-slide.text: The SLC-40 tower's emergency escape is an evacuation slide.
wiki-slc40-slide.quote: In February 2024, SpaceX tested its new emergency escape system for future crewed missions, which uses an evacuation slide instead of the slidewire baskets used at LC-39A.

photo-lightning-towers.text: The four lightning towers stand in two pairs either side of the pad: steel lattice towers with a white mast on top, wires strung between the masts and guyed to the ground.
photo-lightning-towers.note: Read off NASA's 2024 photograph (reference/pad/pad-3.jpg) and SpaceX's 2010 aerial (pad-1.jpg); no source gives the heights, which are estimated from the photograph against the crew tower.

photo-erector.text: The transporter-erector is a steel lattice beam beside the rocket, hinged at its foot by the launch mount, with arms that hold the stack.
photo-erector.note: Read off NASA's photographs of the rocket being raised (pad-3.jpg) and standing on the pad (pad-4.jpg) and SpaceX's 2015 photograph (pad-2.jpg); the arm count and the angle it pulls back are drawing choices.

photo-crew-tower.text: The access tower is a square dark steel tower beside the pad with a swing arm and a white room near its top.
photo-crew-tower.note: Read off NASA's 2024 photographs (pad-3.jpg, pad-4.jpg); the arm is drawn swung away, as for a flight with no crew, and the slide is a plain chute.

wiki-three-engine-burns.text: The boostback and entry burns light three of the nine engines.
wiki-three-engine-burns.quote: by the fourth flight test, in September 2014, SpaceX was reigniting the engines three times to accomplish its EDL test objectives (although only three of the nine engines were used): a boost-back burn, a reentry burn, and a landing burn.

wiki-centre-engine-burns.text: The centre engine lights for every recovery burn.
wiki-centre-engine-burns.quote: If the booster returns to a landing site on land another burn is needed shortly after stage separation to reverse the flight direction of the booster, for a total of four burns for the center engine.

wiki-single-engine-landing.text: The landing burn here uses the centre engine alone, as single-engine landings do; some landings use three engines.
wiki-single-engine-landing.quote: SpaceX opted for a shorter landing burn with three engines instead of the single-engine burns seen in earlier attempts

wiki-fairing-recovery.text: The fairing halves come down under parachutes and are scooped out of the sea to fly again.
wiki-fairing-recovery.quote: Additionally, the fairing halves are scooped out of water after a parachute-assisted landing and can be reflown multiple times.

film-time-factor.text: The readout shows how many times faster than real time the film runs.
film-time-factor.note: The factor is the film's playback rate at that moment (model playbackRate times the film's slow-motion speed); the flight's real times stay those of the model.
